Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007     Gold 

# Gold 

## Recent trends 

The gold price rose fairly steadily from 10 January ($608.40/oz at the pm fix) to 26 February ($685.75/oz).  However while the first part of this rise appeared to be well supported by physical demand, the second stage appeared to be driven largely by speculative interest. Accordingly the stock market turbulence that started on 27 February hit gold as well and the price fell back to a trough of $636.75/oz on March 5 before recovering.  Since then it has been on a largely upward trend, supported by a weakening dollar and stronger oil prices, as well as the tensions over Iran’s capture of UK naval personnel, to end March at $661.75/oz. 

- The World Gold Council reported that total identifiable gold demand in Q4 was 6% higher than a year earlier in tonnage terms and 34% higher in dollar terms.  Allowing for the impact of price turbulence on demand in the early part of the year this brought the fall in total identifiable demand for 2006 to 10%; this was equivalent to a 22% rise in dollar terms, reaching $65.3bn, a third successive annual record. 

- Import data for India and Turkey, along with market reports, suggest that demand for jewellery and related physical markets was reasonably strong in January.  However indications are that it faded in February as the price rose higher.  Market reports indicate moderate demand in March after the price fall. From mid-February, after Chinese New Year and Valentines Day, there has been a dearth of major gold-buying occasions, coupled with a lull in the Indian wedding season. 

- The report of the Committee of Eminent Persons set up to review future financing of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) recommends, among other measures, the sale of 403 tonnes of the Fund’s gold.  With 3,217 tonnes, the Fund is the world’s third largest gold holder.  The 403 tonnes is the gold acquired after the Second Amendment of the Fund’s articles in 1978 (treated separately in the Fund’s accounts from the rest of its holding) and is mainly composed of gold acquired in the off-market transactions of 1999-2000<sup>1</sup> .  The Committee’s report emphasised that any sale “not add to the announced total of central bank selling” and be handled to avoid market disruption.  However, to sell gold the Fund requires an 85% vote of its members in favour. The USA with a 16.83% voting weight has an effective veto, and needs congressional approval to vote in favour.  On two recent occasions congressional sentiment has been against of IMF gold so the proposed sale is far from certain. 

> 1 During these transactions the Fund sold gold to Mexico and Brazil at market prices, these countries then immediately using the gold to repay loans. This enabled the Fund effectively to revalue the gold in its books, a straight revaluation being forbidden by the Fund’s Articles. The implicit profit from the transaction was used to finance the Fund’s share of debt relief for poor count

ries. #### Potential IMF sales will not change overall central bank picture Signatories to the 2nd Central Bank Gold Agreement collectively sold 103 tonnes less than their annual limit during the second year (27 September 05 to 26 September 06) of the Agreement. They look set to sell no more, and probably less, in future years. Meanw hile central banks outside the CBGA are starting to become net buyers, albeit only to a small extent as yet. An element of supply that accounted, at its peak, for over 15% of total supply halved in 2006 and looks likely to decline further. The decline in net official selling means that the proposed sale of 403 tonnes of the IMF's gold, suggested by the Committee of Eminent Persons set up to review methods of IMF financing, can easily be accommodated. The Committee's report indicated that this should "not add to the announced total of central bank selling. That is if it happens. #### Technicals may signal a warning…. From a technical view point, the biggest threat to the continuation of the gold uptrend comes from contrarian (bear) traders, w ith gold now becoming an attractive target. It has risen more or less consistently since mid-1999, offers potential for a major move and is sufficiently liquid to allow the establishment of sizeable positions. The event most likely to pull these opportunistic shorts into the gold market w ill be a strong rally, often called a capitulation rally, w hich marks the last gasp of the bull run. The contrarians w ill bet, w ith some confidence, on the existence of stop loss selling orders and put options beneath the market, w hich w ill be triggered and attract a further w ave of selling on the descent. A sharp rally, an increase in volume, and grow ing open interest as the market falls are likely to be the first precursors of a major trend reversal. A clear double top formation w ould also signal future w eakness - but if the price suceeds in passing the $725/oz peak in May and moves on upw ard a further leg of the bull run could be in view . #### …but fundamentals and other indicators #### suggest further strength Trends in demand and supply, how ever, suggest that the bull run has further to go. The projected rise in mine output w ill be limited by the dearth of exploration in the late 1990s and the long length of time needed to develop new mines. Meanw hile net central bank selling has fallen and there are signs that a number of central banks could turn net buyers. Reduced dehedging w ill add to supply to a certain extent but there is no sign of the substantial return to hedging that w ould be needed for this factor to

become again a major element of supply. Only scrap supply w ill respond to price. Meanw hile investment demand is grow ing and seems to have much further to run. Jew ellery demand, w hile affected by price rises, appears robust enough, supported by a buoyant w orld economy, to underpin any rise in price initiated by investors. A fall in the dollar over the next few months and ongoing political tensions w ould be further price-supportive factors. #### 1980 peak to be surpassed in nominal #### terms - but not in real ones Annual average price, $/oz

Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Gold 5 ## Forecast update: strong fundamentals continue to support price _A fall in supply, growing investor interest and robust underlying jewellery demand resulted in a 36% rise in the gold price in 2006 compared to 2005. Supply and demand trends look set to support a further rise in the price. The extent and strength of future investor interest and the extent to which central banks turn purchasers rather than sellers look set to be the key determinants of how far, and for how long, the price rise continues._ ### **A year of sharp price movements** More than enough data on gold are now available for a full assessment of the year 2006, and what developments during it mean for future prospects. The year was marked by spectacular price movements for gold: the average price for the year was 36% higher than in 2005, the price at the end of December was 24% higher than the price one year earlier, while the year’s high – $725/oz – was 38% higher than the year’s low. The gold market is complex; causality between price movements in gold on the one hand and fundamental supply and demand on the other is neither straightforward nor all in one direction. This article will attempt to disentangle the various threads and draw lessons for the future. Its analysis of supply and demand will draw primarily on the information published by the World Gold Council (based on data compiled by GFMS) since this gives a complete supply and demand picture. Three main elements need to be assessed: the action of investors and their growing, but sometimes erratic, affection for the metal; the sharp reduction in the supply of gold in 2006 compared to 2005; and the reaction of demand for jewellery and industrial products to the impact of the other two elements on the price. ### **The reduction in supply** Logically, it makes sense to start by considering supply since three of the four elements of this are largely unaffected in the short run by price or other economic influences and can thus be considered mainly exogenous. And all three of these exogenous elements reduced supply – one (mine output) marginally but the other two (producer de-hedging and net central ba

nk selling) substantially – compared to 2005. The resulting reduction in overall supply (13%) was thus a key element of the gold market in 2006 and must account for some (but not all) of the rise in the price. Much is talked about constraints on #### Supply fell in 2006 Change from 2005, tonnes

mine output – and indeed there are constraints on it over the next few years – but year-to-year movements are small. In 2006 this fell by just 2%. In contrast there was a very substantial fall in net central bank sales that 6 Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Gold declined by around 50% to 342 tonnes on CRU data (319 tonnes on GFMS/WGC data which include movements in some quasi-official holdings). Sales under the Central Bank Gold Agreement (CBGA) amounted to just 345 tonnes in the calendar year; in the second CBGA year (27 September 2005 to 26 September 2006) the signatories undersold their 500 tonne annual limit by just over 100 tonnes. Outside the CBGA the calendar year 2006 saw limited reported buying and selling which effectively netted out; GFMS estimate that there was net purchasing for quasi-official or undeclared holdings. De-hedging by producers was substantial in 2006 at 403 tonnes (WGC/GFMS figure) compared to just 86 tonnes in 2005; the main, but not the only, component of this being a decision by Barrick, following their acquisition of Placer Dome at the beginning of the year, to unwind most of the Placer hedge book. Barrick/Placer accounted for 285 tonnes of the total dehedging figure. De-hedging (notably buying back or delivering into forward sales) reduces the effective supply of gold to the market since the gold concerned is used to repay loans. All these three elements can be considered reasonably autonomous in the short run. Mine output cannot be adjusted quickly; central bank buying or selling is typically the product of a lengthy decision-making process; and while price does affect the impact of hedging to some extent in the short run, a company’s policy is not something that changes overnight. Of the four elements of supply only scrap responds rapidly to price movements in the short term and 2006 did indeed see a 20% increase in supply from this source, primarily in the first half of the year. This was not enough, however, to offset the fall in the other three components. Basic economic theory dictates that any largely-exogenous fall in supply must, other things being equal, result in a rise in the price, forcing potential purchasers not prepared to tender higher prices out of the market until supply and demand once again match. The extent to which the price has to rise depends on how strong underlying demand is and how resistant buyers are to price rises. The fact that the

price had to rise by as much as 36% compared to 2005 underlines how strong demand was. In this context it is also worth comparing 2006 with 2004. There was in fact little difference in overall supply in these two years: supply in 2006 being just 3% higher than that in 2004. Yet the average price in 2006 was $604/oz, 49% higher than the 2004 level. This therefore indicates the strength of demand for gold, since it would have been the implicit competition between purchasers, accounts for most of the price rise over the two-year period. Between 2004 and 2005 supply increased by 19% but the gold price rose by 9%; between 2005 and 2006 supply fell by 13% and the price rose by 36%. Taking the two years together – in one of which supply rose and in the other it fell, provides conclusive evidence of strong growth in underlying demand for the metal at work. ### **The return of the long-term investor** Here we arrive at the second element of our story: investment. The action of investors is sometimes difficult to analyse, and precise statistical measurement is not always possible. However, at the risk of over-simplification we can divide investors into three categories. The Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Gold 7 first category is the retail investor in bars and coins. In many countries this is quite a small market but it is significant in a few such as Japan, Turkey, India and Vietnam. Specific factors affect each of these markets (for example in ##### Variable trends in retail invesment Vietnam much gold purchase is linked to house buying and other property investment) and buying will be affected by economic and financial conditions in the country concerned. Outside these elements, though, buyers will buy when they perceive the price to be advantageous and expect a further rise. In 2006 there were mixed trends in this sector with overall a small 4% rise in tonnage terms. In India and Vietnam such investment boomed, but Japan saw net selling as many investors who had bought in earlier years took the opportunity to take, often substantial, profits. The second category can be categorised as the speculative buyer, such as hedge funds. The investment horizon of these funds varies but often the most obviously active element in the gold market is made up of those with a short-term speculative horizon. They will be in and out of the market often within a short time period. This is a difficult element to track statistically. Their influence was most evident in the second quarter where they were clearly largely responsible for driving the price up to its $725/oz peak in May – and then driving it down again. The final category of investor is the most crucial for long-term gold prospects. This

is the large investor – private or institutional – with a longer-term horizon. In the 1990s this category of investor almost disappeared from the gold market or was evident primarily as a seller. But over the last few years this has started to change. A combination of factors has caused some longer-term investors to look anew at gold. The political and economic environment has included a number of supportive factors including the fall from 2002 in the US dollar (gold is a dollar hedge), fears over inflation driven partly by rising oil prices (gold is viewed as an inflation hedge) and geo-political tensions (gold is seen as a safe haven). The diversification benefits of adding gold to a portfolio (returns tend not to be correlated with mainstream investment assets) slowly began to be better known. The rise in the price and an appreciation among investors of improving fundamentals in the gold market added to the yellow metal’s attraction. A major factor was the growing interest in commodities generally – some investors have bought gold simply as part of a commodity “package”. And, finally, new investment instruments, notably the Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs), have been developed to make investment easier and cheaper, and to overcome regulatory or legal hurdles. With the exception of ETFs, it is also difficult to capture the action of these investors statistically but a number of indications enable some conclusions to be drawn. First, the major elements of the market to be drawn to gold initially were those hedge or private wealth funds with a long-term perspective (as distinct from the shorter-term more speculative funds) and the 8 Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Gold large-scale individual investor, the latter, an important component of the market, often investing through family funds. Major institutional investors – such as pension and mutual funds, endowments and foundations – have been slower to follow, in part due to the longer-decision making process they are subject to and a cautious approach to changing strategic asset allocation. Information available suggests that they still only account for a small – albeit growing – section of the gold investment market. ##### ETF holdings grow erratically, but they do grow Net inflow s into ETFs, tonnes

Investment in the ETFs is the only inflow that can be easily tracked. Inflows vary from month to month but they do appear to be largely “sticky” holders – in times when the more speculative investor is bailing out, the ETFs only suffer a very modest level of attrition. World Gold Council analysis also indicates that shares in gold ETFs have been mainly bought by “new” investors, so there is little cannibalisation of other forms of gold investment. In 2006 net investment inflows into E

TFs and similar products amounted to 265 tonnes, on GFMS/World Gold Council data, 27% higher than in 2005. 

Together with other buying by long-term investors this section of the market represents a resurgence of demand that was effectively absent for many years; given the limited but slowly growing interest from institutional investors there is potential (albeit nothing is inevitable) for this trend to continue for a good while. 

### **Jewellery – hit by rising prices but with an underlying robustness** 

There are two other forms of demand apart from investment: industrial and dental; and jewellery.  The former accounts for just over 10% of the market.  The major industrial demand is in production of electronic components and this, not surprisingly given the strength of the world economy, has been growing well with demand for gold 11% higher in 2006.  Even allowing for some weakness in other forms of industrial and dental demand, the overall category grew by 7%. 

Jewellery, though, remains the largest component of demand (as measured), accounting for around 70% of the total.  Much demand for jewellery remains price sensitive – reacting badly in particular to price volatility.  Traditionally jewellery in many Middle East and Asian countries, which account for around two thirds of demand, is sold by weight at a price that varies from day to day according to the international gold price.  When the price is volatile buyers will therefore hold back from buying lest they find later that they could have bought at a more advantageous price.  They return to the market once the price is perceived as having stabilised.  Thus in the first half of 2006, jewellery demand suffered due to the volatile and rising price; it was 28% lower in tonnage terms than in the first half of 2005.  In the third quarter as the price began to

stabilise it started tentatively to recover, but was still 9% below year-earlier rates.  In the fourth quarter it was 2% higher than in the fourth quarter of 2005.  Demand was particularly strong in the six weeks from the middle of September to the end of October when the price dipped for a while below $600/oz and buyers rushed to purchase at what was perceived to be an 

advantageous price spurred, in addition, by the approach of Diwali in India and the Eid al Fitr at the end of Ramadan, both traditionally gold-buying occasions. 

The 2% year-on-year increase in Q4 2006 may not appear particularly impressive until one remembers that the dollar price rose by 27% over that period so that in dollar terms buyers were spending 29% more than a year earlier on gold.  Most countries that are major gold markets have currencies linked either tightly or loosely to the dollar so trends in the dollar value give a good indication of the spending trend in national currency terms. 

Reports suggest that January 2007 also saw reasonably strong demand although the higher prices seen in February did deter

buyers.  Because of the way buyers react to price movements, jewellery buyers tend to set the floor to the market (while it is the investor who normally drives the price up from the floor).  Since the gold price started to rise from 2001, jewellery buyers have become accustomed to higher and higher prices providing a rising floor to the market. Currently that floor appears to be comfortably over $600/oz, perhaps in the $620 to $640 range. 

### **And the future?** 

This then is the state of supply and demand in early 2007.  Looking at the future we expect mine output to rise (see _Storyboard_ and Table 9) but the extent of the rise will be limited.  The dearth of gold exploration during the late 1990s has resulted in a limited number of major finds while the length of time to develop a mine, including the permitting procedures, once a discovery has been assessed, can take many years.  There will therefore be a limited rise in supply from this source.  An additional increase will be provided from a reduction in de-hedging.  The combined hedge book of mining companies has shrunk steadily from a peak of over 3,000 tonnes in 2000 to around 1,300 at the end of 2006 (Virtual Metals data).  There is some scope for further reduction but the irreducible minimum must be approaching.  However, at the moment there is little sign of any widespread appetite for increased hedging by gold companies.  There is some new hedging, primarily associated with the financing of new projects, but sentiment in many companies remains firmly against the practice.  Thus for the moment it seems unlikely that a major wave of new hedging will add to supply. 

CRU forecasts that together additional mine supply and the reduction in de-hedging will add over 900 tonnes to supply between 2006 and 2009.  However this will be at least partly offset by much lower net central bank selling.  It seems unlikely that signatories to the Central Bank Gold Agreement will sell up to their limit in future years and, even if plans for a sale of IMF gold come to fruition (not certain – see _Recent Trends_ ), this will still keep overall official selling within bounds.  Perhaps more importantly, it does seem that a trend towards central bank buying has started, albeit it is still very early days.  In recent months it appears that Russia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Qatar have bought gold, as well as, according to GFMS, some purchasing by quasiofficial non-reported holdings.  The amounts concerned are so far small but this could be indicative of the tide turning.  The projections we have for central bank activity (see Table 13) 

10 

Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007    Gold 

assumes that the IMF does sell the proposed 403 tonnes and assume only modest buying by central banks so are conservative.  Nevertheless they suggest that net central bank selling remains under 300 tonnes a year for the next few years. 

Allowing for movements in scrap to be determined by price increases we expect total supply to

peak at not much over 4,000 tonnes in 2008-09. As outlined above, we believe that investor interest in gold will be maintained for the next 2- 3 years; it will remain strong and could intensify. Exchange Traded Funds will continue to spread to different areas of the world (although the US will remain the major market) and attract continuing inflows. We expect some further move of pension and other long-term institutional holders into gold as well as on-going interest from private and family funds. This combined with the limited increase in supply will push the price up further. Jewellery demand will be hurt by the rising price, although we expect some temporary recovery in 2007 from 2006 levels on the assumption that the price is less volatile this year than last and that buyers have now got used to prices in excess of $600/oz. Nevertheless with strong economic growth expected in major markets and rapidly rising income levels in middle-income families in Asian markets we believe that potential demand will be strong enough to support the rise in the price. The key questions for the price forecast are, first, how long this renewed investor interest will last and how strong it will be and, second, the extent to which central banks turn buyers. Our forecast takes the middle ground on investment by assuming that the upsurge in investor interest continues at a reasonably strong pace for another 2-3 years but then fades; as outlined we have made conservative assumptions about central bank buying since there is not yet evidence of a real surge here. It would clearly be possible for either of these to be stronger or weaker than projected with consequent effects on the price.
